# Organiser Dry-Run — §42

**Verdict: PASS**, 8/8 variants, generated by `make dry-run`
(`src/muleguard/cli/dry_run.py`), recorded in
`artifacts/metrics/organiser_dry_run.json`.

This is a rehearsal of the only interaction that decides the competition: an
organiser opens the Validation Lab, drops in a spreadsheet nobody here has seen,
and expects scored rows back. It runs over HTTP against a live backend rather
than in-process, because that is how they will run it, and every way it can fail
is a way that never appears in a unit test — a stray index column, a shuffled
export, resolution fields nobody stripped.

## 1. The mock file

| | |
|---|---|
| Source | the **locked test split** — 1,818 rows no candidate model was ever fitted on |
| Shape | 1,818 × 3,924 after the target column was dropped |
| Target removed | `F3924` |
| Positives withheld | 17 (prevalence 0.935 %) |
| Workbook | `artifacts/dry_run/mock_hidden_validation.xlsx` (sha `07c5fa125c5ee5d1`) |
| Labels | `artifacts/dry_run/mock_hidden_labels.csv` — a **separate file** |

The labels live in their own file on purpose. It makes "the scorer could not
have seen the answer" a property of the filesystem rather than a claim in a
report.

## 2. The seven malformations

Each is something a real export does by accident. All eight uploads were
accepted, scored and sealed; none required a target column.

| Variant | Format | Columns seen | Result |
|---|---|---:|---|
| `baseline` | .xlsx | 3,937 | PASS · compatibility 99.97 |
| `baseline_csv` | .csv | 3,937 | PASS · compatibility 99.97 |
| `shuffled_column_order` | .csv | 3,937 | PASS · compatibility 99.97 |
| `extra_columns` (`analyst_notes`, `export_batch`, `Unnamed: 0`) | .csv | 3,940 | PASS · compatibility 99.97 |
| `f3912_present` | .csv | 3,937 | PASS · compatibility 99.97 |
| `resolution_fields_present` (F3898/F3899/F3913/F3914/F3915) | .csv | 3,937 | PASS · compatibility 99.97 |
| `category_changes` (unseen category in a **selected** feature) | .csv | 3,937 | PASS · compatibility 99.85 |
| `missing_optional_fields` (40 non-required columns dropped) | .csv | 3,897 | PASS · compatibility 99.97 |

All 120 required features resolved in every variant
(`n_missing_required: 0`, `schema_completeness: 1.0`), of which 117 came from
the file and 3 are `MG_*` meta-features derived row-wise from the file's own
columns after the target was withheld.

## 3. What the variants actually prove

Scoring successfully proves very little on its own. The stronger claim is that
the five variants which *should* be indistinguishable produced **byte-identical
prediction files** — same SHA-256, `cc9f65a1945b407b…`:

| Variant | vs baseline | Why it must hold |
|---|---|---|
| `shuffled_column_order` | identical | column order is not information |
| `extra_columns` | identical | columns the model does not consume are ignored |
| `f3912_present` | identical | **F3912 is quarantined — supplying it changes nothing** |
| `resolution_fields_present` | identical | **post-resolution fields are quarantined — supplying them changes nothing** |
| `missing_optional_fields` | identical | columns the model does not consume are not needed |

The two bold rows are the Feature Availability Firewall being tested where it
counts: at *inference*, on a file that carries the forbidden columns anyway. The
firewall is usually argued from the training configuration; here it is measured
from the output.

**The control that makes those five rows evidence:** `category_changes` put an
unseen category into a feature the champion genuinely reads, and its predictions
**differ** (compatibility also drops, 99.97 → 99.85). Without that row, five
identical hashes would be equally consistent with a harness that never reached
the scorer at all. An earlier revision of this probe changed a text column that
was not among the 120 selected features, all eight hashes matched, and the green
result meant nothing — which is why the control is now checked and the release
gate fails if it stops differing.

## 4. The model did not move

Bundle fingerprint `afd0dc1d8fc02eb9` before the first upload and after the
last — the same joblib SHA-256, winner, feature count, calibrator, policy
thresholds and data fingerprint. Scoring an upload never writes back into the
model. This is checked after **every** variant, not once at the end.

## 5. Offline comparison against the withheld labels

Order enforced by the Sealed Validation Protocol (UPDATE 11/12): schema →
shield → predictions → hash → *only then* labels.

- Sealed `10:59:04.490653Z`, revealed `10:59:38.459657Z`
- Seal verified at reveal: **true**, state `METRICS_REVEALED`

| Metric | Value |
|---|---:|
| PR-AUC | **0.7263** |
| ROC-AUC | 0.9665 |
| Lift over prevalence | 77.7× |
| Recall@25 / @50 / @100 | 0.706 / 0.706 / 0.824 |
| Precision@25 / @50 / @100 | 0.480 / 0.240 / 0.140 |
| MCC @ top-100 | 0.327 |
| Rows / positives | 1,818 / 17 |

0.7263 on the locked test against 0.7690 OOF is the ordinary, expected direction
and size of drop. It is reported as measured.

## 6. Why this metric cannot have leaked into training

Four independent reasons, in the order they take effect:

1. The rows are the **locked test split** — held out of every fold, asserted
   absent from `cv_folds.parquet` by `run_oof`.
2. The target column was dropped from the workbook **before it left the
   process** that built it; the labels went to a different file.
3. The API withholds any label column it finds *before* scoring
   (`sealed.withhold_target`), so the scoring frame never contains one.
4. Labels were supplied only at reveal time, against a prediction file whose
   SHA-256 had already been written down. The reveal endpoint re-hashes and
   refuses on mismatch, so the metric provably describes predictions that
   existed before any label was read.

Nothing in this run retrained, tuned, recalibrated or re-thresholded anything
(UPDATE 3).

## 7. One real defect this found

The first run rejected all six CSV variants with `422 ComputeError`. The cause
was in `_parse_upload`: the CSV schema was inferred from 200 rows, so a column
that is numeric for the first 200 rows and carries a stray non-numeric value at
row 900 aborted the entire upload. On a 3,924-column file that is close to
certain, and it would have meant the organiser's file being refused over a
single cell — the worst failure this route has.

Fixed in `src/muleguard/api/routes_upload.py` with `_read_csv_tolerantly`:
sniff 200 rows, then scan the whole file, then read every column as text, then
tolerate ragged lines. Coercion downstream turns an unparseable cell into a
null, which the imputer already handles. A 422 turns it into no submission at
all.

## 8. Reproducing

```bash
.venv/Scripts/python.exe -m uvicorn muleguard.api.main:app --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8001
make dry-run
```

Enforced by release gate check `organiser_dry_run_passed`, which requires three
separate facts — every variant scored, the invariances held, and the sensitivity
control differed — because any one alone is satisfiable by a broken harness.
